title: The name on the meat
hook: the animal is killed swiftly, with Allah's name, a sharp blade, and mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday: nikah, and the question of dating: what's agreed, and what's discussed. Your line was a feeling isn't a sin.

Supermarket meat arrives on a foam tray under plastic, and the moment the animal died is somebody else's business. Islam doesn't let that moment disappear. Halal meat isn't just about which animals. It's about how. There's a name that has to be said, and a blade that has to be sharp. And a hadith puts one word over the whole thing, a word you wouldn't expect at a slaughterhouse.
screen: `A FOAM TRAY UNDER PLASTIC.` → `NOT JUST WHICH ANIMAL, BUT HOW.` → `A WORD YOU WOULDN'T EXPECT.`

segments.voice: The word is dhabihah, an animal slaughtered in the prescribed way. The core is simple. The one slaughtering says the name of Allah, usually bismillah, Allahu akbar. Then one swift cut across the throat with a very sharp blade, so it's over quickly and the blood drains out, since the Qur'an forbids eating blood. The name comes from the Qur'an: in Surah al-An'am, believers are told to eat of what Allah's name has been said over, and not of what it hasn't. Some teachers explain the name as a reminder that the life being taken was never ours: it's taken with permission, not by right. Then the word. Sahih Muslim reports, from Shaddad ibn Aws, that the Prophet ﷺ said: Allah has written ihsan on everything. Ihsan means excellence, beauty, doing a thing as well as it can be done. So when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade, and spare the animal suffering. Other reports go further: don't sharpen the knife where the animal can see, and don't slaughter one animal in front of another. The same collections tell of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog, and a woman punished for starving a cat. Mercy even here, at the hardest moment. Muslims differ on some modern questions: scholars disagree about stunning before slaughter, and about whether ordinary meat from Jews and Christians, whose food the Qur'an calls lawful, still counts today. Under the debates sit the plain basics: say the name, keep the blade sharp, and be kind.
screen: `DHABIHAH — THE NAME AND THE CUT.` · `EAT WHAT HIS NAME WAS SAID OVER.` · `IHSAN IS WRITTEN ON EVERYTHING.` · `SCHOLARS DIFFER ON MODERN QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `MERCY EVEN HERE.`

segments.voice: Bukhari reports that the Prophet told a young boy at his table: say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you. So picture your next meal, and pause before the first bite. If you pray, you can say bismillah, in the name of Allah; if not, remember that something, a plant or an animal, went into this plate, and someone grew it, caught it or cooked it, and give one breath of thanks.
Dhabihah. Meat slaughtered in the prescribed way: Allah's name, a swift cut with a sharp blade, and mercy. Today's word.
Your line: mercy even here. Ihsan is written on everything, even this. Day one hundred forty-five, done.

howItsDone: Halal meat comes from an animal slaughtered with Allah's name spoken, one swift cut with a sharp blade, the blood drained, and care to spare it suffering; Muslims also say bismillah before eating.
